title: Battle Sign -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Battle sign is a clinical finding characterized by ecchymosis over the mastoid process and is most commonly associated with significant blunt head trauma. The presence of Battle sign often indicates an underlying basilar skull fracture, particularly involving the temporal bone, and may be accompanied by additional findings such as hemotympanum, cerebrospinal fluid otorrhea or rhinorrhea, and cranial nerve deficits. This physical sign reflects the tracking of blood from the posterior cranial fossa to the mastoid region and is not limited to injury of the mastoid or posterior cranial vault alone. Battle sign is associated with an increased risk of intracranial hemorrhage, vascular injury, and traumatic brain injury, requiring prompt recognition and thorough evaluation. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment supported by neuroimaging, most commonly computed tomography, to identify fractures and associated intracranial pathology.

title: Battle Sign -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance clinician competence in the timely recognition, evaluation, and management of Battle sign following head trauma. Participants gain a structured approach to physical examination, appropriate selection of imaging, and identification of associated injuries requiring urgent intervention. The activity emphasizes evidence-based management strategies, including neurologic monitoring, consultation thresholds, and prevention of secondary brain injury. Collaboration among the interprofessional healthcare team, including emergency medicine, neurosurgery, radiology, otolaryngology, and nursing, is highlighted as essential for coordinated assessment, timely intervention, and improved patient outcomes in individuals presenting with signs of basilar skull fracture.

title: Battle Sign -- Introduction
content: Battle sign is defined as bruising over the mastoid process; this bruising, retroauricular or mastoid ecchymosis, is typically the result of head trauma (see Image. Battle Sign). [1] The battle sign is named after Dr William Henry Battle, who first described it in the late 1800s. He was an English surgeon who initially described the ecchymosis in 17 patients who had head injuries with fractures to the posterior aspect of the skull base. His description noted that to develop the sign, there was significant head trauma, which may indicate significant internal injury to the brain and not just the posterior cranial vault or mastoid. [2]

title: Battle Sign -- Etiology
content: One of the most important issues associated with Battle sign is that it takes 1 to -2 days for the sign to appear and is thus not helpful in the initial management of head trauma. [2] The naming of the Battle sign has caused much confusion over the years. Many believe that the sign derives its name from fighting or battling as a mechanism for sustaining the injury, rather than from Dr Battle. Additionally, although Dr Battle is credited with the sign and has his name on it, he was not the first to note it. Sir Prescott G Hewett, an English surgeon, had actually written about the association before Dr Battle. [3] Battle sign may be confused with a spreading hematoma from a fracture of the mandibular condyle, which is a less serious injury. [4] Another issue surrounding Battle sign is that there was a recent case report that showed mastoid ecchymosis associated with hepatic encephalopathy in the absence of trauma. This case means that Battle sign may not be as specific for head trauma as initially thought. However, further research is needed on the association between hepatic encephalopathy and mastoid ecchymosis. [5]

title: Battle Sign -- Epidemiology
content: Basilar skull fractures are present in only 4% of patients with a severe head injury. [6] There is no reported increased predilection among any sex or any race. Battle sign typically correlates with blunt head trauma; this is most commonly accidental but may also be present in nonaccidental head trauma, including in child abuse. Overall, most skull fractures are linear and are more common in children. The temporal bone is involved in the majority of skull fractures (45%), followed by basilar skull fractures (20%). When a depressed skull fracture occurs, it is usually an open fracture, which generally necessitates surgery as soon as possible.

title: Battle Sign -- Pathophysiology
content: Battle sign is prominent when there is a fracture of the petrous temporal bone; it may also be associated with rhinorrhea and bruising over the eyes (raccoon eyes). Depending on the severity of the head trauma, the patient may also present with loss of consciousness and a depressed Glasgow coma scale.

title: Battle Sign -- History and Physical
content: Battle sign presents as ecchymosis over the mastoid process, located behind the ear. This condition is typically associated with tenderness in the area. Other findings that may be seen that indicate basilar skull fracture include raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis), hemotympanum (which is the presence of blood in the tympanic cavity of the middle ear), facial nerve injury, and laceration of the external auditory canal. [3] Battle sign is often present with a basilar skull fracture. The presence of Battle sign correlates with a positive predictive value of greater than 75% for the presence of an associated basilar skull fracture. Results from multiple studies have shown that the Battle sign has a positive predictive value of 66% for intracranial lesions and 100% for skull base fractures. [4]

title: Battle Sign -- Evaluation
content: Battle sign is a clinical sign; no further evaluation is needed to diagnose it. However, given that Battle sign correlates with an underlying skull fracture, imaging is typically warranted when Battle sign is observed. The initial evaluation is with a non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan; however, linear or nondisplaced fractures may not be detectable and may require further imaging. [7] If the presentation is delayed and infection is suspected, contrast-enhanced CT or magnetic resonance imaging may be useful. Importantly, check for nasal bleeding to rule out cerebrospinal fluid leak; this may be assessed by measuring tau, transferrin, or glucose levels.

title: Battle Sign -- Treatment / Management
content: In general, the treatment following a skull fracture depends on the type of injury. Patients with linear fractures who have no neurological deficits and have a GCS of 14 or higher can be discharged home safely after a period of observation in the emergency room. However, the patient must be available for follow-up if they become symptomatic. Children with linear fractures need to be admitted overnight, irrespective of the absence/presence of neurological deficits.

title: Battle Sign -- Treatment / Management
content: Surgery is usually required when patients have depressed skull fractures. The current consensus is that if the depressed segment is more than 5 mm below the inner table of adjacent bone, the patient should undergo surgery to elevate that bone segment. Other indications for surgery include underlying hematoma, gross infection/contamination, and dural tear with pneumocephalus.

title: Battle Sign -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients with an open wound or delayed presentation should be treated with tetanus toxoid and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Basilar skull fractures are secondary to trauma, and thus, management requires a thorough trauma evaluation. Admission for observation is usually necessary, with subsequent management determined by the fracture. [8]

title: Battle Sign -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Battle sign may be positive rarely in other conditions such as hepatic encephalopathy. [5]

title: Battle Sign -- Prognosis
content: The Battle sign itself will fade and heal with time, although it may take several weeks for the ecchymosis to disappear. When Battle sign is present, the patient is more likely to have a slower than expected recovery from a head injury. [3]

title: Battle Sign -- Complications
content: When patients present with Battle signs, it is vital to rule out associated cervical spine injury. Data reveal that 15% of patients with a basilar skull fracture have an associated cervical spine injury.

title: Battle Sign -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Following surgery, patients will require monitoring for intracranial hematoma, venous sinus thrombosis, and mental status. Those discharged without surgery should be seen in the clinic within 24 to 48 hours to assess the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and mental status. All patients who undergo surgery need to have a repeat CT scan within 6 to 8 weeks to rule out the presence/absence of an abscess. Other reasons to follow up include the presence of seizures and neurological deficits.

title: Battle Sign -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: The patient should receive education about observing for CSF otorrhea and fever.

title: Battle Sign -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: An interprofessional team of nurses, allied health professionals, and physicians that interacts and reports to one another is the most effective approach to managing traumatic injuries. Battle sign, when identified by any member of the team, should be reported as it is potential evidence of significant head trauma.
